demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Threat.value: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

Negative Appraisals.value: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation
I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: For a trauma of accidentally causing serious injury to another, the appraisal that the patient's own body has been permanently damaged is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile unless she was also physically injured, which is not reflected elsewhere. The other selected appraisals center on self-blame and humiliation, which fit this trauma type, but this item introduces a different trauma meaning without supporting threat, memory, trigger, or strategy content.

issues.item: Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
issues.explanation: The threat items imply a broad, ongoing danger/vulnerability pattern focused on personal safety (restricted safe places, nighttime checking for safety). For a trauma involving accidentally causing serious injury to another person, this is hard to reconcile unless there is additional trauma involving danger to self; the threat content would more plausibly center on fear of causing harm again, moral threat, or social/legal consequences.

issues.item: Threat: Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
issues.explanation: Within the formulation, the only active edge is Threat → Negative Appraisals, so threat and appraisals should show a plausible thematic link. Here the threat items center on physical safety and hypervigilance, while the appraisals center on guilt, self-blame, and humiliation about having caused harm. That disconnect suggests the selected threat items are not well aligned with the appraisals for this trauma type.

issues.item: Threat: Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
issues.explanation: For trauma of accidentally causing serious injury to another, the threat profile is poorly matched: nocturnal checking for safety and inability to relax in safe places imply an ongoing danger/victimization-based fear response, but the appraisals center on guilt and self-blame about causing harm. That combination is hard to reconcile clinically without any items about fear of legal retaliation, being attacked, or another external threat.

issues.item: Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
issues.explanation: Within the formulation, the only active link is Threat → Negative Appraisals, so threat items should plausibly feed the selected appraisals. Here the threat items suggest current physical danger/hypervigilance, whereas the negative appraisals are predominantly moral self-judgment and shame. Humiliation in particular is weakly connected to the stated threat content, making the cross-node pattern clinically incoherent.

vignette:
Margaret has worked as a model for over four decades, and at sixty-six she still booked the occasional editorial for women her age—until the accident. She was driving home from a late shoot, exhausted, when she failed to see a cyclist turning through the intersection. The impact threw him across the hood; he survived, but with a broken pelvis and internal injuries that left him unable to walk for months. Margaret was not physically hurt, but from that moment her body began to live as though it were the one that had been struck.

In the weeks afterward, she found she could not relax, even at home with the door locked. Her muscles stayed tight, her jaw clenched, and every sudden noise—a car horn, a bicycle bell through an open window—sent her heart racing. She had difficulty concentrating during bookings. In the middle of a pose, her attention would slide to the memory of the impact, and she would lose focus, missing the photographer’s directions. Her body felt constantly on alert, waiting for another catastrophe, though she knew she was safe.

What frightened Margaret most was what this constant vigilance seemed to prove about her character. Because she could not settle her body or her mind, she became certain that somebody else—someone more composed, more worthy—would not have gotten into this situation in the first place. The hyperarousal, she believed, was a mirror of her fundamental incompetence. She felt permanently humiliated by what happened, as though the accident had stripped away the poise she had built a career on, and now her twitchy, jumpy body broadcast her shame to everyone. And under it all, guilt gnawed: she would never forgive herself for not doing more to stop the accident—for not being more alert, for not seeing the cyclist sooner. The tension in her chest felt like a punishment she deserved.

The more her body stayed on edge, the more the self-criticism sharpened. Driving became impossible; she stopped completely, relying on hired cars or friends to take her to jobs, which limited which bookings she could accept. She avoided the intersection and any news story about cycling accidents, but the alertness followed her indoors. At a recent shoot for a retirement-living campaign, the photographer asked her to look calm and content. She tried, but her grip on the prop teacup was white-knuckled, and she kept scanning the studio windows for movement. She left early, apologizing. Afterwards she spent the evening replaying the accident, convinced that her inability to relax was proof she should never have been behind the wheel that night.

Months passed, and the cycle tightened. Her daughter finally insisted she see someone, and Margaret agreed not because she believed she deserved relief, but because she could no longer bear the cost of the constant alertness on her work and her few relationships. She came to therapy with her hands clasped in her lap, describing the accident in a flat voice, then adding, “I know I’m supposed to move on, but I can’t even sit still without feeling like something’s about to go wrong—and that just proves I never should have been driving at all.” She is most afraid that the therapist will agree with her—that she is permanently damaged—but underneath that fear is a fragile hope that someone might show her a way to be less afraid of her own body’s signals without having to erase the guilt she carries for the man she hurt.
